title: Five Traits Marriage-Minded Young Women Should Look For in a Man
gist: Freya India argues marriage-minded young women should prioritize character over viral checklists like height and income, naming five traits: clear intentions, protectiveness, online and offline fidelity, shared values, and belief in lifelong marriage. She backs each with IFS, Wheatley, UVA and academic survey data linking these traits to marital happiness and stability.

insights.claim: Social media pushes young women toward superficial dating standards such as men over six foot earning six-figure salaries, while what actually predicts marital happiness and stability is largely character.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Highlights how social-media norms shape dating-market expectations and household formation.
insights.quote: much of what predicts marital happiness and stability involves character
insights.locator: Of course, other factors are important

insights.claim: The author frames marriage not as a market search for the best product but as building a lasting life together.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A counter-narrative to app-driven optimization culture in dating.
insights.quote: Marriage is not about finding the best product on the market but about building a life together that lasts.
insights.locator: But this is not how marriage should work.

insights.claim: Modern dating is marked by confusion over intentions—'talking stages,' 'situationships,' and keeping a 'roster' of multiple people—which the author argues women should reject.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Ambiguous dating norms delay coupling and household formation.
insights.locator: In modern dating, there’s a lot of confusion

insights.claim: Per the 2025 IFS/Wheatley Institute report For Better, husbands who completely agree their marriage is one of the most important parts of their lives have 234% higher odds of being very happy in marriage.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Quantifies the payoff to commitment for marital stability.
insights.quote: have 234% higher odds of being “very happy” in their marriages than less devoted husbands
insights.locator: He should have clear intentions throughout

insights.claim: Psychologist Scott Stanley's 'sliding vs. deciding' distinction holds that couples should actively decide each relationship stage—exclusivity, engagement, marriage, children—rather than drift into them.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Deliberate transitions are linked to more durable unions.
insights.locator: There’s also a difference between “sliding” and “deciding,”

insights.claim: An IFS/YouGov survey of Americans 18-29 found more than 70% of young men say men should protect women, a similar share of young women agree, and 64% of liberal young women concur despite egalitarian dating attitudes.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Shows durable traditional preferences beneath egalitarian Gen Z norms.
insights.quote: More than 70% of young men say that men should protect women, and a similar share of young women agree
insights.locator: In fact, a recent IFS and YouGov survey

insights.claim: Per For Better, wives who say it is definitely true their husbands are protective are 137% more likely to be very happy, and husbands with highly protective wives are 61% more likely to be very happily married.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Protectiveness, including loyalty, correlates strongly with marital satisfaction for both sexes.
insights.quote: wives who said it was “definitely true” that their husbands are protective were 137% more likely to be very happy
insights.locator: So look for someone who makes you feel safe

insights.claim: Weakened societal boundaries have created new forms of online infidelity such as 'micro-cheating'—deleting DMs or liking other women's bikini pictures—and pressure on women to tolerate it.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Social platforms are reshaping relationship norms and conflict.
insights.locator: Online, too, there are new forms of infidelity

insights.claim: A 2017 longitudinal study by Samuel Perry and Cyrus Schleifer of over 2,000 married Americans found those who started watching porn were more likely to divorce; models suggest a 20-year-old starting porn has a 51% divorce chance versus 9% for one who doesn't.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Frames online adult content as a material driver of marital instability.
insights.quote: a 20-year-old who starts watching porn has a 51% chance of divorce, compared to 9% for one who doesn’t
insights.locator: Look for a man who does not watch porn

insights.claim: The National Marriage Project's 2019 iFidelity report found married and cohabiting Americans who crossed three or more online boundaries were 26 percentage points less likely to be very happy in their relationships.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Online behavior is a measurable risk factor for relationship quality.
insights.quote: were 26 percentage points less likely to be “very happy” in their relationships
insights.locator: As it happens, strong online boundaries

insights.claim: The author advises women to avoid men who follow porn stars and OnlyFans influencers, and that a man with a porn problem should be honest and willing to change.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Reflects growing cultural backlash against creator-driven adult content platforms.
insights.locator: But you should have a guy’s full attention.

insights.claim: IFS's The Devout Difference report found 78% of value-aligned Catholic and Protestant spouses report happy marriages versus 36% of non-aligned spouses, naming value alignment the single strongest predictor of marital satisfaction.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Religious and value homogamy strongly predicts marital stability.
insights.quote: 78% of value-aligned Catholic and Protestant spouses say they are in happy marriages, compared to only 36% of non-aligned spouses
insights.locator: It's also important to look for one

insights.claim: Per For Better, husbands who regularly attend church with their wives have 212% higher odds of very happy marriages.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Joint religious practice is a large correlate of marital happiness.
insights.locator: It's also important to look for one

insights.claim: Popular culture, including the Call Her Daddy podcast where Alex Cooper said the answer to 'could I do better than my husband' is 'always yes,' treats marriage as conditional and divorce as a celebrated fresh start.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Media narratives may erode marital permanence norms, with downstream effects on family stability.

insights.claim: According to The Devout Difference, belief in marital permanence strongly predicts satisfaction, and couples sharing a strong lifelong commitment report the highest marital happiness; children of divorce face higher anxiety, depression and school struggles.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Permanence beliefs are linked to stable households and better child outcomes.
